content.thinking:
I need to piece together the timeline carefully without inventing any figures, using placeholder names in braces for people involved. The deploy at 18:44 removed the empty-month guard, but there's a conflict between when the flag was actually toggled — the log shows flag evaluations happening before the reported toggle time of 18:49:26, which needs reconciling.

The root cause looks like the guard removal exposing a ZeroDivisionError for shoppers with past-but-not-current-month purchases, with the flag controlling exposure to that path. I should flag the timing discrepancy as an assumption rather than asserting certainty, and note that rollback was never successfully executed, so the deploy itself was never fully confirmed as the trigger even though the evidence points that way.

I need to lay out the error metrics (percentage during the incident, peak, baseline), duration, and detection delay without hardcoding specific numbers, and separately list the ruled-out factors (the earlier deploy with normal baseline errors) versus the contributing factors, like the apparent lack of test coverage for shoppers with no purchases in the current month.

For next steps, I'm thinking through action items: adding regression tests to catch this scenario, making the rollback path actually reachable since it failed during the incident, and introducing staged rollout for feature flags rather than full exposure. I'll number these sequentially after the existing ones and tie each back to the specific contributing factor it addresses, keeping the proposals modest and grounded in what was actually observed.

I also want to be careful with how I cite timestamps and identifiers — using labels like change record or log references rather than raw numbers where possible, and flagging any discrepancy between when the flag was switched versus when it actually took effect in the logs as something worth noting in my assumptions.

action_items.item: Add a CI regression test for the monthly spend figure with a shopper who has past purchases and none this month, and require it to pass before a change to spend_summary.py can merge.
Give Argus a working path to roll back a deployment when the deployment platform is unreachable, or a documented manual fallback, and check that the path works on a schedule.
Roll out the monthly-spend-feature flag, and flags like it, in stages, with an automatic revert if the error rate rises. Do this before the flag goes to all traffic.
Add an alert on the rate of ZeroDivisionError log lines from the account page, so a new exception is flagged before the {rule_waits} error-rate rule fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw failed account page requests. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, and the paging rule fired at {alert_raised}. A share of traffic equal to {errors_rise} failed that would otherwise have succeeded.
Each failed request raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at spend_summary.py:47 in the spend-summary code. The account page turned that error into a failed response.

The function average_spend_per_item_this_month divides the month's total by the number of purchases found this month. After the later deploy, that number could be zero while the total was still non-zero, for a shopper with past purchases and none this month.

The deploy removed the empty-month guard that returned zero, and redefined 'this month' from recorded_at. Nothing in the record shows a test or review catching that the division could now hit an empty list. A static reading of the code (unverified, since nothing ran it) says an idle-this-month shopper is ordinary input, not a rare edge case.

The monthly-spend-feature flag exposed the broken path. Once the flag was on, evaluations went through the spend-summary path, and errors began at the onset. Switching the flag off cleared the errors, which confirms the flag was the route to the fault. The earlier deploy was ruled out: it went out hours before the onset and the error rate stayed at its baseline until the later deploy. The flag provider's history showed a flag change, so the flag was not unchanged. The guard removal in the deploy is the fault the flag exposed. The rollback of the deploy never ran, so the deploy's role was not confirmed by reversing it.

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that covers a shopper with past purchases and none this month, and no review check was seen that caught the removal of the empty-month guard before the deploy reached production. The fix adds such tests only after the incident.
The rollback of the deployment could not be made because the deployment platform was unreachable, so Argus could not undo the deploy that carried the fault. Only the flag revert was available.
The monthly-spend-feature flag sent traffic through a code path that had just changed. No staged rollout or health check on the flag was seen, so the fault reached a large share of requests at once.
The paging rule waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding, and the alert came at {alert_raised}, after the onset at {began}. No faster signal on the ZeroDivisionError log line was seen.

input.executive_summary: For a short period, a large share of account page requests on the shop failed. The error rate rose from {errors_before} before the incident to {errors_while_broken} on average while it was broken, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. It lasted {duration}. The people affected were shoppers who had bought before but not yet this month, and for them the account page returned an error. A code change had removed a safety check on a spend calculation, and a feature switch then sent traffic through that calculation. Argus tried to roll the deploy back, but the deployment platform could not be reached. It then switched the feature off, and the error rate returned to normal. A draft fix that restores the check has been proposed and still needs review.

got_lucky: The flag could be reverted even though the deployment platform could not be reached, so the mitigation did not depend on the platform.
The deploy is still in place with the guard removed. The flag is the only thing keeping traffic off the broken path until the fix merges.
went_well: Argus found the change that removed the guard, read what it changed, and proposed a fix as a draft pull request.
When the rollback could not be made, Argus moved on to the flag revert, which was confirmed. The paging rule stopped firing and metrics were back to normal at {back_to_normal}.
went_wrong: The rollback of the deployment failed because the platform was unreachable, so the deploy itself was never reverted.
The change record shows the flag switch at {P3.1}, after the onset at {began}. The logs show the flag already evaluating on at the onset. The record is inconsistent about when the flag changed.
Errors reached {errors_at_worst} at worst before the flag was reverted.

input.root_cause: The later io-shop deploy removed the guard in average_spend_per_item_this_month that returned zero for a shopper with no purchases this month, and changed how "this month" is decided. For a shopper with past purchases but none this month, the function divides by an empty list and raises ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, so the account page request fails. The monthly-spend-feature flag sent traffic down that path. Reverting the flag stopped the errors, but the deploy was never rolled back, so the deploy as the origin was not tested by a rollback.
